newsitem.title: UK: Monkeys boost meningitis vaccine hopes.
newsitem.headline: Monkeys boost meningitis vaccine hopes.

text.p: Monkey trials may have boosted the chances of producing an effective long-term vaccine for meningitis, scientists reported on Thursday.
Meningitis, a life-threatening inflammation of the tissues around the brain, currently kills one in 10 of its victims. It is most prevalent in sub-Saharan Africa.
The current vaccines against meningitis do not provide long-term protection and cannot be used at all on infants under the age of two.
But Peter Fusco and colleagues at North American Vaccine in Beltsville, Maryland, have sought to tackle the problem, the New Scientist magazine reported.
They have tinkered with the sugary polysaccharide molecules that poke out from the surface of bacteria and protect them from their host's immune system.
The vaccine they developed in monkey trials worked on all three meningitis serogroups. Booster vaccinations given months later triggered ever stronger immune responses, they said.
Fusco told the magazine that this suggests the vaccine might give much longer protection than existing ones.
"Hopefully, the body remembers having seen the bacteria before," Fusco said.
